INTRODUCTION

Whether it be city planning or school curricula, tension over how history is represented,
remembered and taught has gripped the American social and political landscape over
the past several years. The 2020 Black Lives Matter uprisings brought renewed and critical
attention to public commemoration, particularly the abundance of statues, memorials and
place-names dedicated to the legacies of the Civil War, and how these offer one-sided
historical narratives. The nation-wide struggles over the function of public commemoration
have emphasized how many for ms of remembrance are also contingent upon forgetting,
and rely on erasing or silencing synchronous histories of violence, injustice and resistance
that infor m a complete telling of history. Urban landscapes have always held a particularly
relevant role for their potential to construct, reinforce and complicate historical
narratives, ethnic identities and political representation. The tension between the city as a
constant environment and that which is also constantly being re-made, reinforces social
geographer David Harvey’s notion of the “right to the city,”, one of the most fundamental
and neglected human rights: the ability to exercise collective power to reshape processes
of urbanization (Harvey, 2003).

Since urban landscapes are immediate reflections of cultural, social and political contexts,
polarizing discourse around race and identity has inevitably spilled out into the city streets.
Who and how different histories and identities are written into our environments generates
tension with different for ms of place-making, such as street names, monuments and statues.
These are especially complex in urban settings, where layers of community build upon each
other in often infor mal and nuanced ways. Commemoration has implications for civic identity
and belonging in urban neighbor hoods. Discussions over whether a statue should be removed
or remain intact are often lightly concealed debates over whose history and whose identity
should be represented in the physical fabric of the city. The histories that we tell affir m and
entrench power relations. Nuanced historical representation is an important aspect of social
justice.

Cityscapes are an accumulation of contested memories. Historical narratives are embedded
in physical spaces and objects, and in the words of Pierre Nora, these “sites of memory”
shape our sense of the past. According to the art historian Erika Doss, we now live in the
midst of a “memorial mania” (Nora, 1989; Doss, 2010). Street naming integrates history and
commemoration into the spatial politics of the city, which is important to note as part of
processes of gentrification. This holds especially true in Los Angeles, where commemoration,
as both a process and an event, archives the complicated interactions and different struggles
for agency, power, and identity that make up the history of the entire city. Commemoration
politics in Los Angeles today seeks to represent the city’s landscape by more accurately
remembering its past, in order to understand all that makes up its present.

In order to address these issues of memory, power and identity in the urban landscape, this
report focuses on street names as for ms of commemoration, using Los Angeles as a case

5

[PDF page 6]
study. Within broader contemporary debates over commemoration, street names have
arguably received less attention than statues or monuments. However, they are some of the
most common markers of history that we encounter in our everyday lives. Commemorative
street names are all around us, even if we don’t necessarily recognize them as such. They
shape our sense of the past by marking, legitimizing and making “official” certain versions of
history in everyday life. They celebrate some communities, people, and events, while erasing
others. Their power lies in their ordinariness, and their ability to “effectively implicate politics
and ideology into the practices of everyday life and ordinary urban experiences” (Azaryahu,
2009: 56).  These “official” versions of history might seem totally detached from ideological
contexts, which allows them to make certain interpretations of the past seem both familiar
and self-evident. At the same time, in processes of subtle resistance, some streets are known
infor mally by different names.

The commemorative street names of any city are arguably interesting, and provide a key
to understanding what and who has been deemed worthy of remembrance over time. Our
focus on Los Angeles reflects the central place that cars and streets play in the city’s mythos.
Angelinos famously spend hours in their cars everyday and have an aversion to walking. Much
of this reflects the booster history of land development in Los Angeles, and was by intentional
design. The TV and Film industry has played its own part in shaping this narrative into reality.
Some streets gain iconic cultural status through movies: Mulholland Drive (2001), Sunset
Boulevard (1950), and Melrose Place (1992-1999). Los Angeles therefore offers an alter native
vision to public commemoration: our monuments lie not in statues, but in streets.

This report focuses especially on street re-naming as a civic process and a policy concer n.
Within national debates over who is commemorated and who is forgotten, re-naming has
become a hot topic. Locally, as the recent LA Mayor’s Report, About T ime, made clear, public
participation in crafting historical narratives is an important for m of civic engagement. The
historical geographer Derek Alder man contends that the renaming of streets in ways that are
inclusive relates to “the broader rights of people to participate in the production of place
and to have their cultural identities and histories recognized publicly” (Alder man and Inwood,
2013). Street names in Los Angeles have become embroiled in debates over what and who
is worthy of public remembrance. Because the City Council has oversight over street names,
our civic leaders are in fact actively involved in shaping our sense of the past. Over the past
twenty years, over two hundred proposals to rename streets have appeared before the city
council.

As Los Angeles seeks to create a more inclusive commemorative landscape and to deepen
our civic history, this report contributes a much-needed historical perspective to the issue of
street renaming. We focus on the following questions:

1.  Over the past twenty years, who and what has been prioritized for commemoration in Los
Angeles street names, and where have those changes taken place?

2.  What is the role of infor mal vs. for mal commemoration?

3.  How does the identity of commemorated individuals intersect with spatial dynamics of the
city?

RESEARCH METHODS

We conducted archival research within the LA City Council archive and identified
council files related to street name changes between 2000 and 2022. This date range was
selected because it includes data from two for malized processes related to street-name
commemoration which require council approval: ceremonial signs and street name changes.
For each motion, we created a spreadsheet that included basic infor mation such as council
file number, new name of street / ceremonial sign, the date the motion was approved (if it
was approved), and the primary mover of the motion. We also created categories for theming
the data, which included the type of subject commemorated (person, place, business, etc),
the reason for commemoration (arts and culture, civil service, representation of a minority
group, etc), and the identity of the person being commemorated (woman, race/ethnicity/
nationality, sexual orientation, etc).

Translating our data into maps required the addition of geographic infor mation to each
feature, and a substantial amount of data cleaning, analysis, and visualization. The necessary
spatial data was obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau (roads), L.A. City Geohub (council
districts), and Los Angeles T imes (neighbor hoods). Location infor mation provided by the City
Council files was used, along with the Census’ road data, was used to map each ceremonial
sign and renamed feature; these features were then updated to include their council district
and neighbor hood. Using this organizational approach, we were able to filter and analyze the
dataset, and create choropleth maps in QGIS and Adobe Illustrator.
DATA AND FINDINGS

Data Overview

From 2000 - 2022, we located over 264 examples of adopted name changes (there were
an additional 42 ceremonial signs and 14 street name changes that were proposed but
not adopted). These name changes fell into three categories: for mal street name changes
(such as the change from Rodeo Street to Obama Blvd), the naming of newly established
streets, and ceremonial signs. While the first two categories involve the naming of a roadway,
ceremonial signage is a for m of naming layered on top of the directional street name.
For example, the intersection of First Street and Grand Avenue, next to the Walt Disney
Concert Hall in Downtown LA, is named Er nest Fleischmann Square in commemoration of
the renowned manager of the Los Angeles Philhar monic. Many ceremonial signs name
intersections as “squares”, thereby creating a new name for an intersection of two streets
both of which keep their original street names. Ceremonial signs are more infor mal than
street name changes. Of the 264 name changes, 182 were ceremonial signs and 82 were

7

[PDF page 8]
name changes. As the graphs below reveal, once the process of ceremonial signs was
for malized, the use of ceremonial signs increased. They are now the dominant for m of street
commemoration in Los Angeles.

The difference between ceremonial signs and street name changes is largely procedural.
That is, erecting a ceremonial sign requires engagement with a different civic process than
changing or establishing the name of a street. The technicality of this difference is important
for thinking more broadly about the relationship between power and commemoration.
Deliberate engagement with one type of commemoration over the other might have
something to say about who and what has the agency to commemorate, or be
commemorated.

Is everything commemorative?

Not all street names are commemorative. In addition to categorizing examples of street
renaming according to for m and process, they can also be categorized as commemorative
or non-commemorative. Ceremonial signs are, by their nature, always commemorative. They
tend to have specific and explicit reason(s) for commemoration, based for example on a
desire to represent ethnic identity, gender, civil service, a person’s contribution to a particular
field or cause, or a combination of these reasons.

Like ceremonial signs, commemorative street name changes represent specific reasons for
renaming. These are typically to commemorate a person of importance to the city, country
or for a significant figure within mainstream culture more broadly. Examples of this type of
commemorative street renaming include the renaming of Rodeo Road in the Baldwin Hills/
Crenshaw neighbor hood to Obama Boulevard in 2018, or the changing of a stretch of
9th street in Downtown Los Angeles to James M. Wood Boulevard in 1999. It also includes
commemorative street names that are tied geographically to businesses or other sites, such as
Universal Studios Boulevard (changed from Coral Drive in 2000), LMU Drive and L.A. Live Way.

Commemorative naming has a very strong presence in Los Angeles. Of the streets renamed
between 2000 and 2022, all (182) ceremonial signs and 28 street name changes were
commemorative (for a total of 210 commemorative features). While some streets are (re)
named with explicit commemorative intentions (Obama Blvd, L.A. Live Way), others are
changed due to issues related to public safety, logistics or other more specific reasons. In our
dataset, we identified these as non-commemorative for mal street name changes. These are
changes that were petitioned and/or occurred in city council archives, but were not explicitly
tied to cultural or identity representation. Instead, these changes encompass everything from
maintaining an architectural style, to a political or personal decision, to a desire to improve
emergency services. By analyzing this data, our report posits that commemoration is a
complex reflection of different power dynamics in Los Angeles. Even when a name change
is not explicitly commemorative, it nonetheless maintains political, social, and cultural value
in the city - and that this is its own type of commemoration. Engagement with the name
changing process requires financial investment, demonstrating an awareness and desire to
influence the city landscape and people in some way. It is a kind of commemoration that has
important implications for the role and value that private developers, real estate and housing

CASE STUDY
Non-commemorative street name changes

City council file 99-0013 provides an apt record of the relationship between real estate and
street naming. In 1998, the Pacific Palisades Highlands Homeowners Association successfully
petitioned the city council for the changing of a series of 8 streets in the Pacific Palisades
neighbor hood to use the Spanish suffix “Via” in place of “Calle” when referring to the street
title. This included changing the names of streets Calle de Nancy, Calle de Cielo, and Calle
Deborah to Via Pacifica, Via la Costa, and Via Las Palmas, respectively.

Spanish place naming has a complicated history in Los Angeles. While many Spanish street
names represent specific individuals or communities, many more were named as part of the
early 20th century Spanish Revival movement. This aesthetic movement, which encompassed
both architecture and place-naming, invoked a romanticized colonial past. The romantic
appeal of Spanish names, which invoke an imagined past, continue to have appeal today,
especially in wealthier white neighbor hoods.

The petition on file records the homeowners association proposed reasoning for the change:
“to provide a more Spanish flavor” to the neighbor hood, to be “much easier to pronounce
and communicate to others”. That the streets had already used a Spanish suffix (“Calle”)
and wished to change so to be more linguistically “legible” to non-Spanish speakers and
more “geographically descriptive” of the area suggests that street naming can be used as a
kind of display; to connote an ethnic identity and linguistic power difference, or as an agent
in anglicizing and historical whitewashing. Here, historical “Spanishness” was appropriated
in order to mark the socio-economic status of the neighbor hood. The lack of a substantive
reason behind this change, and the success of its petition has a lot to say about the way
that naming both establishes community in Los Angeles - a city where neighbor hoods both
define and segregate communities. Even

PROCESS AND POWER

What is the role of informal vs. formal commemoration?

The processes for the different types of commemorative naming practices are different
and those differences impact the who, what and why of commemoration. The comparison
between the process of ceremonial signs and for mal street renaming illustrates the
ways in which a for mal vs. infor mal process are reflected in for mal vs infor mal objects of
commemoration.

The processes for renaming streets and erecting ceremonial signs are quite different.
Renaming streets is a more arduous process. It requires that a majority (minimum of 51 %) of
the property owners abutting the street that is being petitioned for a name change must be
submitted with the street name change application (LAAC Section 19.6 – Petition for Change).
Similarly, a $5,000.00 fee deposit is required (LAAC Section 19.6 – Petition for Change) until
the total cost is calculated. The outcome of a for mal street name change also means that
everyone living, working, or owning businesses or properties on that street must change their
address. This consequence means an additional level of engagement from those living on the
street that is being renamed, as opposed to erecting a ceremonial street sign which has no
real tangible effect on property owners on the street where the ceremonial sign is placed.

The process of erecting a ceremonial street sign reflects its lesser impact on the property
owners along the stretch of street or intersection that is being commemorated. Ceremonial
signs are free - there is no fee to request or erect them. Residents can petition their city council
member who, if they agree with the request, will bring a motion to the city council. The motion
is voted on and, if it passes, a ceremonial sign is erected.

For mal and infor mal place naming have existed side by side for much longer than the period
covered by this report. At times, failed street renaming proposals have resulted in the naming
of squares, intersections or other public spaces in ways that do not impact existing street
names. This dynamic is illustrated by the case of Raoul Wallenberg Square. In 1986, the City
Council received a petition to rename Fair  fax Avenue “Raoul Wallenberg Blvd” after the
Swedish envoy who saved thousands of Jewish lives during the Nazi occupation of Hungary.
The proposal was rejected. However, two years later, the City Council agreed to name the
intersection of Fair  fax Avenue and Beverly Boulevard “Raoul Wallenberg Square.” In 2003, the
practice of adopting names in a more infor mal or ceremonial fashion (without requiring a
street name change) was for malized with a process for establishing ceremonial signage. This
process constituted a civic recognition that urban spaces accumulate many narratives over
time, or layers of memory, and that these layers can be officially marked by the existence of
multiple names (Huyssen, 2003).

Process matters

While ceremonial signage facilitates the presence of multiple narratives, our dataset suggests
that there is a correlation between who and what is being commemorated, and type of
commemoration. Ceremonial signs are more likely related with themes that we might think
of as “infor mal” than for mal street names. Two common categories that emerged in all
commemorative for ms were “civil service” and “community engagement.” A person honored
for civil service might include a Judge of the US Court of Appeals or a State Assemblymember
while someone honored for community engagement might include a children’s advocate
who led the neighbor hood Boys and Girls Club or a pastor who also worked to prevent
insurance redlining in South Los Angeles. As illustrated by the chart below, ceremonial signs
had a much higher rate of commemorating this infor mal type of community service. Between
2000 and 2022 there was a much higher percentage of street name changes commemorating
civil servants than those involved in less for mal for ms of community service. The number of
people commemorated for their identity or representation of a minority group was much
higher for ceremonial signs than street name signs. This might suggest that commemoration
based on identity may be too contentious to get through the more intensive process of street
renaming and is thus more closely associated with the easier process of ceremonial signs.

archive and these physical signs may abound in the landscape, but how meaningful are they

Per haps these signs are more meaningful at hyperlocal level, particularly when they
commemorate people for local impacts on their communities. Unlike the example given

someone of city-wide influence - many other ceremonial signs commemorate people who

program, and gang prevention and intervention program, among other things. His impact on

The spatial dynamics of formal and informal naming

The distinction between “for mal” (street renaming) and “infor mal” (ceremonial sign)
commemoration is bor n out not only in ter ms of who is being commemorated, but where
they are commemorated. This point is elaborated by spatial analysis. Choropleth maps
show the geographic distribution of for mal street renaming and ceremonial signs, and invite
questions about how these processes have impacted the urban fabric of Los Angeles. This
distribution was tabulated for both city council districts and neighbor hoods. Since members
of the LA City Council are largely responsible for commemoration in the urban landscape,
the for mer is particularly useful for analyzing the political dynamics of commemoration.
However, neighbor hoods were used as the main spatial unit of this project because, unlike
administrative boundaries, they describe the geographic, historic, and socio-economic
associations that define communities, and are more relevant to the daily lives of Angelenos.

Neighbor hood-level maps show that these “infor mal” and “for mal” processes have distinct
spatial distributions, in addition to their other differences. On the one hand, ceremonial
signage is clustered in the city’s historic center: Downtown and Central-Alameda are each
home to 8% of all ceremonial signs, and Historic South-Central has the third-largest share. On
the other hand, Venice and San Pedro — both on the city’s edge — have the most for mally-
renamed streets (8%). Downtown is the only neighbor hood in Central L.A. with over 5% of
for mally renamed streets, and this level is matched by the San Fer nando Valley neighbor hoods
of Panorama City, Sylmar, and Lake View Terrace. In short, the infor mal, ceremonial renaming
process is far more common in the city center, while the distribution of the for mal renaming
process is broader and more diffuse. This patter n was also observed in the district-level maps:
Districts 9 and 10 have the largest share of ceremonial signs, and Districts 7, 11, and 15 have
the most for mally-renamed streets. However, while the maps show clear differences in these
processes’ distributions, they cannot tell us why these differences exist.

Infor mal commemoration with ceremonial signs is more likely to recognize similarly
“infor mal” topics, like non-gover nmental community service or representation of a minority
group, than for mal renaming. There are power dynamics inherent in choosing who gets
commemorated and where. With the exception of Downtown, ceremonial signs are most
abundant in neighbor hoods that have historically been excluded from the map of power
— the spatial distribution of economic and political power and privilege — by redlining and
the entrenched segregation it produced (T ijerina, 2019). Our data suggests that historically
marginalized neighbor hoods lack for mal renaming, and the placement of ceremonial signs
in such neighbor hoods may be intended to “fill out” the commemorative landscape. This
phenomenon is most pronounced in Central-Alameda and Historic South-Central, but can
also be observed in Koreatown, Ver mont Square, South Park, and Florence. Of course, not
every neighbor hood adheres to this patter n: neighbor hoods that are famous (Hollywood),
represented by a frequent primary mover (San Pedro), or power  ful and historically significant
(Downtown) also have large shares of ceremonial signs.

At first glance, the map showing for mal street renaming by neighbor hood appears to
be almost the inverse of ceremonial sign distribution, showing a marked trend towards
suburbanization. Unlike ceremonial signs, which are, by nature, commemorative, only about
40% of for mal street renaming is undertaken for commemorative purposes; the remainder
is split between administrative and public safety changes, street name establishments,
and street (re)naming in conjunction with (public or private) development projects. Most
commemorative for mal street name changes fall into the categories of “Arts and Culture” or
“Civil Service”. Downtown is home to a full 20% of these types of changes — nearly twice as
many as the runner-up, Studio City. In contrast to infor mal, ceremonial renaming, these results
suggest that for mal renaming is most common in centers of for mal power, and most likely to
recognize less divisive subjects that are already entrenched in the commemorative canon, like
politicians and the arts.

Meanwhile, our datamaps demonstrate that non-commemorative for mal street name
changes are concentrated in suburbs like Venice, San Pedro, Sylmar, Lakeview Terrace, and
Panorama City — nearly as far from Downtown as you can get within Los Angeles city bounds.
In each of these neighbor hoods, the majority of for mal renaming is undertaken for other
reasons. Our report understands street names as carrying cultural, political and social value.
Public naming, as a for m of representation and power, thus maintains political significance,
even (and uniquely so) in the records of non-commemorative street name changes. Levels of
engagement with the civic process of renaming are concentrated differently across the city,
which helps visualize how where and how street names are changed is also related to why
they are changed.

Ultimately, commemoration, whether for mal or infor mal, is the result of a complex interaction
between numerous influences. While neighbor hood dynamics and demographics play an
important role, ceremonial signage is also strongly influenced by City Council Members, and
the large percentage of ceremonial signs in districts of frequent primary movers, like Jan Perry
and Joe Buscaino, illustrates the impact a single person can have on the commemorative
landscape.

Nevertheless, our results demonstrate a clear link between marginalization and infor mality,
and power and for mality. However, questions remain. Is the placement of ceremonial signs
in neighbor hoods that have been historically marginalized and redlined reparative of past
injustices, or is the reliance on the infor mal process a reflection of continued marginalization?
How and by whom are these new names encountered, and what is their impact — on
individuals and communities, from the hyperlocal level to the national stage? Are they meant
to reflect and encourage a sense of belonging among current residents, or are they markers
of disappearing communities? Finally, what infor ms the decision over which process, for mal or
infor mal, a renaming proposal will go through?

CASE STUDY
Neighbor  hood power & identity “Nor  mont Terrace” to
“Harbor Village”

Name changes and discourses around crime, poverty and housing are intimately connected.
A common feature of contemporary urban development, prestige naming helps to legitimize
and naturalize processes of displacement, gentrification, privatization and commodification
(Madden, 2017).

City council file 97-1244 documents the changing of 9 streets within a four-block radius in the
Harbor City neighbor hood in Southwest Los Angeles. The name change coincided with the
redevelopment of Nor mont Terrace, a 400-unit housing project built by the city in 1942 largely
for veterans. Nor mont Terrace was fully owned and operated by the Housing Authority of Los
Angeles as public housing. In 1997, Nor mont Terrace was shut down, redeveloped and re-
managed by a public-private partnership with Related Califor nia, one of the largest private
housing developers in the state. Under the new management, the previous infrastructure
was upgraded but also restructured: of the 800 new units built in 1997, only half of them
were reserved for low-income families. The other 400 units were sold, at market rates, as
condominiums. Today, Nor mont Terrace is known by a different name: Harbor Village. Harbor
Village is a “gated community rich in amenities and convenience”.

The council file includes the petitions for street name changes used during this process
of redevelopment. In order to disassociate the Nor mont housing project from a stigma
of poverty, the new management had to repackage the environment. The renaming,
rebranding and repackaging of the landscape assisted the broader shift in privatizing the
urban landscape, and targeting the effects of poverty and structural disinvestment, rather
than its roots.

“Nor mont Terrace” would cease to exist in the city landscape in 1997. Instead, “The once
crime plagued project [would] become a model for redeveloping public housing and
revitalizing depressed neighbor hoods”. Yet, even as renaming “Nor mont Terrace” to “Harbor
Village” sought to address patter ns of violence, it also simultaneously enforced them: “some
people say they feel like we’re in prison because it’s so regulated” remarked Gloria Moralez, a
43-year old retur ning resident of Nor mont Terrace, tur ned Harbor Village . “We’re not allowed
to barbeque car ne asada or wash our cars in front of our homes”.

CASE STUDY
Power, Commemoration, and Identity: African American
Commemoration

A case study of African American representation in our dataset illustrates the connections
between identity, politics, and commemoration in Los Angeles. Over the past twenty years,
there has been a concerted effort to name streets after African American people. African
American commemorative features (including street names and ceremonial signs) make
up about half of our dataset, which is striking because African Americans make up only
about nine-percent of Los Angeles’ population. However, 97% of the African-American
commemoration identified in our study takes the for m of ceremonial signage, demonstrating
the for mal/infor mal dichotomy discussed above.

We mapped African American commemorative features and found that Historic South-
Central had the largest share (11%) of renamed features commemorating African Americans,
and Central-Alameda and Ver mont Square each had 10% of all African American
commemorative features. Central-Alameda, Ver mont Square and Historic South-Central are
all part of LA City Council District 9, so it makes sense that this district had the highest share
(45%) of renamed features commemorating African Americans.

Using 2020 voting data as a proxy, we mapped African American distribution across Los
Angeles and overlaid that data on top of the distribution of African American commemorative
features. Based on the 2020 data, it appears that there are more African Americans living
in areas south and west of the neighbor hoods with the highest number of commemorative
features.

Below we consider two possible factors – the change in neighbor hood demographics over
time and city council politics – that may help explain the trends in commemoration illustrated
by our maps.

Changing demographics may precipitate acts of commemoration in order to preserve history
or celebrate the past of a changing neighbor hood. While 2020 voting data demonstrates
that fewer African Americans live in Central Alameda than, say, Leimert Park, maps
created by USC Center for the Study of Immigrant Integration as part of their 2016 report
titled, “Roots|Raíces: Latino Engagement, Place Identities, and Shared Futures in South Los
Angeles”, demonstrate the larger demographic shifts that occurred in South Los Angeles
from 1970 to 2010. This data shows that Historic South Central and Central Alameda, the
two neighbor hoods with the highest rate of African American commemoration, were home
to a high percentage of African Americans in the 1970s and 80s; however, by 2010, both
neighbor hoods were more  than 80% Latinx.

We situate this data alongside the commemoration of Black leaders from the community
to suggest that there may be a connection between the two. The people and places
commemorated between 2000 and 2022, through the use of mostly ceremonial signs,

SUMMARY

Our analysis of street renaming in Los Angeles 2002-2022 has revealed five main points:

1.  In ter ms of who and what has been prioritized for commemoration in Los Angeles street
names over the past twenty years, there are some clear trends, which seem to relate
directly to local identity politics and efforts to recognize groups traditionally excluded
from dominant historical narratives. African Americans have been disproportionately
commemorated, but their commemorations have also been disproportionately infor mal.
There has been a clear trend towards a local focus, with individuals recognized for civic
and community service.

2.  Commemoration through street renaming in 2000-2022 was spatially uneven. Certain
politicians and neighbor hoods have prioritized commemoration. The commemorative
landscape reflects a racially segregated city. This often reflects the historic characteristics
of a neighbor hood. Spatially, renaming trends also reflect economic disparities. Wealthier
neighbor hoods tend to have more access to for mal street renaming than poorer
neighbor hoods, where ceremonial signs are more prevalent.

3.  Since 2000, the rise of ceremonial signs has been a significant trend in commemorative
street name changes. This more infor mal for m of commemoration has led to a hyper-local
focus in ter ms of who and what is being commemorated. With a streamlined petition
and approval process, ceremonial signs made the process of infor mal street naming
more accessible. This infor mal commemoration has been important to filling out the
commemorative landscape. On the other hand, at a city level, ceremonial signs might be
less impactful because ceremonial names are not the names that we use in our everyday
spatial vocabularies. People know streets by their official names.

4.  Erasure and forgetting are implicit in the process of renaming. Some street renaming re-
writes neighbor hood histories through efforts at “rebranding.”

5.  Street name changes have a strong relationship to identity politics and the dynamics of
demographic change. Ceremonial signs document not only people, but also the history
of neighbor hoods. They plant deep history in the landscape: ceremonial signs have a
prominent place in neighbor hoods with strong ethnic histories and that are changing.

CONCLUSION: THE FUTURE OF RENAMING

At the heart of Harvey’s declaration of a  “right to the city” lies a belief in changing ourselves
by changing the city. In other words, the city is the ultimate environment to engage with
history, and by shaping the city, we can be active participants in shaping the narratives and
environments of our lives.  Commemoration, as both a process and an event, helps people
and communities understand, represent, and celebrate their identities and assert historical

27

[PDF page 28]
agency in relationship to one another. In doing so, the landscape of the city becomes a
crucial dimension of broader struggles for social justice.

In the past several years, commemoration has become an especially relevant and hot-
button issue in mainstream culture and politics. The tensely divided American “culture wars”
over issues like naming, language and education indicate that understanding history is a
necessary part of pursuing social justice. Remembering and commemorating are a particular
way of expanding history to not only include more voices, but to complicate the voices we
already have. The loud resistance to these changes demonstrates that people do recognize
the power that public commemoration has in our lives. In Los Angeles, like cities all over the
country, we have inherited a vastly unequal commemorative landscape. The means through
which we try to change it must pay particular attention to the nuance and complexity
of historical representation. So long as this historical representation (or the lack thereof)
continues to influence communities and culture in the present, it is clear that these struggles for
agency, identity and power will remain increasingly relevant in our daily lives.

Striving for a more inclusive and just commemorative landscape requires our commitment to
three principles:

1.  Access is key: There is a benefit in creating more opportunities for accessible
commemoration. When the process of street renaming was made more accessible in
2003 with a for mal process for ceremonial signage, it was used to commemorate people
important to local communities. The number of signs adopted every year since 2003 has
increased. The process is being used, and it reveals a need for more accessible for ms of
commemoration.

2.  Strive for processes that facilitate the existence of multiple narratives: Commemoration can
and should be nuanced, just like history itself. Rather than swapping out one narrative for
another, or changing commeoration in order to replace the community that was with the
community that is, we should strive for multiple narratives and even accept dissonance
(Ranciere, 2011). Commemoration is an important part of how we can peel back the
layers of history to include more voices in conversation, rather than opposition, to one
another. Ceremonial signs are a good example of how to engage in layering. They fill out
the Los Angeles landscape by adding to it. Because they do not officially change street
names, ceremonial signs are an interesting case study for thinking about commemoration
as a way to encapsulate and preserve change. This is arguably a productive way of
dealing with the relationship between history and identity politics. Especially in a city as
diversely segregated as Los Angeles, layering establishes a strong groundwork for different
racial and ethnic communities working together, rather than against each other.

3.  Address power imbalance: The different for ms and options for public commemoration
establish a power imbalance in the commemorative landscape (in ter ms of who is
recognized, where and how). Ceremonial signage fills out the landscape, but it does not
address the power imbalance. The additive option, while facilitating multiple narratives,
also creates a hierarchy. The balance between infor mal and for mal renaming needs to be
actively considered, with options for making for mal street renaming more accessible.

Street whose name is an ordinal number

Not to be confused with [Route number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route_number "Route number").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Philly10thStreet.jpg/250px-Philly10thStreet.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philly10thStreet.jpg)

[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia")'s 10th Street written in English and Chinese

A **numbered street** is a street whose name is an [ordinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_number_(linguistics) "Ordinal number (linguistics)"), as in _Second Street_ or _Tenth Avenue_. Such forms are among the most common street names in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), but also exist in other parts of the world, especially in Colombia, which takes the system to an extreme, and the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East"). Numbered streets were first used in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-1) and now exist in many major cities and small towns. [Grid-based naming systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_name#Grid-based_naming_systems "Street name") usually start at 1 (but sometimes at a higher number or even at zero), and then proceed in numerical order. In the United States, seven out of the top ten most common street names are numbers, with the top three names being "2nd," "3rd," and "1st" respectively.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-2) Streets named "0th" are quite uncommon, however, but do exist (sometimes spelled out "Zero Street") (like [0 Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0_Avenue "0 Avenue") in [BC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada), and negative numbered streets (i.e, "−1st", "−2nd", etc.) are extraordinarily rare. Fractional numbered streets exist in some places, such as 10+1⁄2 Street in [Springfield, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Illinois "Springfield, Illinois").

Some cities also have lettered street names. For example, [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), in addition to having numbered streets, also has streets identified as a letter followed by "Street," going as high as the letter W. [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") has avenues titled "Avenue" followed by the respective letter of the alphabet, such as Avenue D. The idea for such a system was developed by [Pierre Charles L'Enfant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Charles_L'Enfant "Pierre Charles L'Enfant"), who devised the system for Washington.

The numbered street system is criticized for taking away the individuality from a community that a named street would provide.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-google-3)

[Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland, has numbered streets in the north-central part of the city. The numbered streets in Baltimore do not begin with 1, but rather start with **20th Street** just north of and parallel to [North Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Avenue_(Baltimore) "North Avenue (Baltimore)"), the former northern boundary of the city, and what is viewed by many today is the northern boundary of [Downtown Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Baltimore "Downtown Baltimore"). The numbered streets, which go as high as **43rd Street**, correspond with the first two digits in the addresses of the north–south streets they cross. Unlike in Washington, where the numbered streets run north–south, Baltimore's numbered streets run west–east. All begin their names with either "West" or "East," depending on which side of [Charles Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_Route_139 "Maryland Route 139") the block is located.

Some of Baltimore's numbered streets are well known for various reasons. 28th and 29th streets, a [one-way pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-way_pair "One-way pair"), are the only numbered streets to have an [interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interchange_(road) "Interchange (road)") with [I-83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jones_Falls_Expressway "Jones Falls Expressway"). They use the numbered designations to the east of the expressway, and to the west, they merge into a six-lane road known as [Druid Park Lake Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druid_Park_Lake_Drive "Druid Park Lake Drive"). [East 33rd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Street_(Baltimore) "33rd Street (Baltimore)") was the location of the now-demolished [Baltimore Memorial Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_Memorial_Stadium "Baltimore Memorial Stadium"), home to the [Baltimore Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_Orioles "Baltimore Orioles") for 38 years and the [Baltimore Colts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Indianapolis_Colts "History of the Indianapolis Colts") for 31. West 34th Street is the location of the annual [Miracle on 34th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracle_on_34th_Street_(Baltimore) "Miracle on 34th Street (Baltimore)"), where residents on one block of the street open their porches to tourists to view their holiday decorations. **West 40th Street** is the location of [The Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rotunda_(Baltimore) "The Rotunda (Baltimore)") shopping mall, and it merges into West 41st Street, which crosses over, but does not have an interchange with, I-83 into [Television Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_Hill,_Baltimore "Television Hill, Baltimore") and is the only numbered street in the city west of I-83.

#### Chicago

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Numbered_street&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Chicago")]

Main article: [Roads and expressways in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roads_and_expressways_in_Chicago "Roads and expressways in Chicago")

The City of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") is set on a grid with eight "standard" city blocks per mile. Some blocks are further divided in half. A standard block has 100 address numbers, meaning there are 800 numbers per mile. Chicago address numbering begins downtown at [State Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_(Chicago) "State Street (Chicago)") and [Madison Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Street_(Chicago) "Madison Street (Chicago)"); State Street is 0 east and west, and Madison Street is 0 north and south. Major streets a mile apart have address numbers that, for the most part, are multiples of 800.

The south side of the city uses numbered east–west streets, although older streets that were already named retained their names, particularly in the [Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Loop "Chicago Loop"). As stated above, Chicago house numbers are generally assigned at the rate of 8 blocks to a mile. The only exceptions are from Madison to 31st Street, just south of downtown.

The first two main numbered roads in the system were renamed for historical figures after the numbering system was adopted. Roosevelt Road (previously 12th Street and renamed for [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt")) is one mile south of Madison with 12 blocks to the mile, Cermak Road (previously 22nd Street and renamed in memory of assassinated mayor [Anton Cermak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Cermak "Anton Cermak")) is two miles south of Madison with 10 blocks to the mile, and 31st Street (3100 S) is three miles south of Madison with 9 blocks to the mile. South of 31st Street, the pattern of 8 blocks to the mile resumes, with 39th Street the next major street, 47th after that, and so on.

The numbering within Chicago is continued in many suburbs south of the city proper. For instance, [Chicago Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Heights,_Illinois "Chicago Heights, Illinois") has a 185th Street, set on the same numbering scheme.

Chicago's numbered street system was established in 1911 by legislation that made Madison Street the base for the numbering of east–west streets, and State Street for north–south streets.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-google2-4)

As a general rule, the only numbered streets in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland,_Ohio "Cleveland, Ohio") run generally north–south, while streets that run parallel to the [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") shoreline (generally east–west) have names rather than numbers. [Public Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Square,_Cleveland "Public Square, Cleveland") in downtown Cleveland separates east- and west-numbered streets, with the numbers increasing in both directions as one travels further away from Public Square, in a system initiated in 1906.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-5) Conforming east–west roads are given a name, rather than a number, and the suffix "Avenue." Where an avenue crosses Ontario Street or the [Cuyahoga River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuyahoga_River "Cuyahoga River"), its name changes, meaning that a numbered street does not intersect a given avenue more than once. For example, stating a location as "65th and Detroit" implies West 65th Street, since Detroit Avenue changes to Superior Avenue when it crosses the river. Non-conforming streets are suffixed with names other than "street" or "avenue," e.g., West Boulevard, Old River Road, Martin Luther King Jr. Drive. Geographic idiosyncrasies in certain parts of the city mean that this is by no means an absolute rule but generally applies within the city proper. The street numbering extends from West 233rd in [North Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Olmsted "North Olmsted") to East 367th in [Eastlake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastlake,_Ohio "Eastlake, Ohio").

[Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver") has two systems in place in two distinct areas of the city. Downtown Denver's diagonal street system technically begins with 4th Street near Auraria Campus, underneath the Colfax Avenue viaduct. The system then counts up northeastward from 4th Street to 40th Street. The diagonal system meets the normal numbered grid at various points, with the termination of the downtown system at 40th Avenue and 40th Street in the Five Points neighborhood.

The second system is a typical East/West layout, with directional indicators. First Avenue is adjacent to Ellsworth Avenue in Central Denver; the series extends to 168th Avenue in unincorporated [Adams County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_County,_Colorado "Adams County, Colorado"). Exceptions include [Colfax Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colfax_Avenue "Colfax Avenue"), which takes the place of 15th Avenue, and Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard, which generally takes the place of East 32nd Avenue. The designations _East_ and _North_ are generally not used unless needed. Building numbers on cross-streets reflect the street numbering; for example, 1800 Colorado Boulevard would be at the corner of 18th Avenue. (1800 South Colorado Boulevard is outside the area of numbered streets.)

In [Greater Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area"), numbered streets go into the three digits, with varying, overlapping sets of numbered streets. The area has roads that are named as a number followed by "Street" that runs west–east, and a number followed by "Avenue" that runs north–south. All these streets start their names with NW, NE, SW, or SE, depending on where they are in relation to the center of [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami "Miami").

In the Miami suburbs, some numbered streets and avenues are paired with a parallel "Court", "Drive", "Place" or "Terrace"; while in the same area, other sets of numbered streets and avenues exist with lower numbers, such as in Hialeah, where W 68th St is also designated NW 122 St [](https://maps.google.com/?ll=25.885713,-80.351&spn=0.023359,0.042272&t=m&z=15). This is known to lead to confusion among some, especially non-locals.

Similar numbering systems are used throughout the state of Florida, such as in [Gainesville](https://maps.google.com/?ll=29.630883,-82.418447&spn=0.022568,0.042272&t=m&z=15), [Ocala](https://maps.google.com/?ll=29.171124,-82.253008&spn=0.045341,0.084543&t=m&z=14), [Panama City](https://maps.google.com/?ll=30.22062,-85.627892&spn=0.011218,0.021136&t=m&z=16), and [Jacksonville](https://maps.google.com/?ll=30.246148,-81.720858&spn=0.011215,0.021136&t=m&z=16).

[Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Avenue "Fifth Avenue") and E. 57th Street in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan")

The [Commissioners' Plan of 1811](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners'_Plan_of_1811 "Commissioners' Plan of 1811") laid out the grid that covers most of [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") today. Most east–west streets (which actually run southeast–northwest) are named "___th Street", and a few major north–south streets (which actually run northeast–southwest, roughly parallel to the island's long axis) are named "___th Avenue".

The highest-numbered [street on Manhattan Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_streets_in_Manhattan "List of streets in Manhattan") is 220th Street, and the highest-numbered street in the Borough of Manhattan is 228th Street.

The Manhattan numbered street grid continues north in The [Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"), where the highest numbered street is West 263rd Street on the border of [Yonkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonkers,_New_York "Yonkers, New York"). The only numbered avenue in The Bronx is a continuation of Manhattan's [Third Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Avenue_(New_York_City) "Third Avenue (New York City)").

In Queens, the melding of various grids from pre-consolidation villages resulted in repeat numbers, for example, 31st Street, 31st Place, 31st Lane, and their perpendicular counterparts 31st Avenue, 31st Road, and 31st Drive. Streets, Places and Lanes run north to south, while Avenues, Roads, and Drives run east to west. Avenues run from 2nd Avenue in Whitestone to 165th Avenue in Howard Beach. Streets run from 1st Street in Astoria to 271st Street in Glen Oaks.

In [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), there are ten sets of numbered streets ([unprefixed numbered streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Brooklyn_streets,_1%E2%80%93101 "List of Brooklyn streets, 1–101") as well as North, South, East, West, Bay, Brighton, Paerdegat, Plumb, and Flatlands numbered streets), along with [numbered avenues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Brooklyn_avenues,_1%E2%80%9328 "List of Brooklyn avenues, 1–28") up to 28th Avenue and [letter avenues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_avenues,_Lettered_A%E2%80%93Z "Brooklyn avenues, Lettered A–Z") up to Avenue Z. Manhattan's [Alphabet City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabet_City,_Manhattan "Alphabet City, Manhattan") consists of Avenues [A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_A_(Manhattan) "Avenue A (Manhattan)") through [D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_D_(Manhattan) "Avenue D (Manhattan)").

The [Rockaways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockaway,_Queens "Rockaway, Queens") section of Queens has streets prefixed with the word _Beach_. However, street signs in this area typically identify this prefix using only the letter B (e.g. ["B 116 St"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockaway_Park%E2%80%93Beach_116th_Street_station "Rockaway Park–Beach 116th Street station")). The neighborhood of [Broad Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Channel,_Queens "Broad Channel, Queens") also has its own network of numbered roads, prefixed with East or West, relative to [Cross Bay Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_Bay_Boulevard "Cross Bay Boulevard").

The closest cross street to a given [building number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_number "Building number") in Manhattan can be estimated using the [Manhattan address algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_address_algorithm "Manhattan address algorithm").

The highest-numbered street in all of New York City is 271st Street, in [Glen Oaks, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Oaks,_Queens "Glen Oaks, Queens").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-7) 704th Street in [Orangeburg, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orangeburg,_New_York "Orangeburg, New York") is the highest-numbered street in the [Greater New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area "New York metropolitan area") area, and at one point was the highest-numbered street in the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-10) The highest-numbered Avenue in Manhattan is the obscure [Thirteenth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_Avenue_(Manhattan) "13th Avenue (Manhattan)"), on Gansevoort Peninsula in the Hudson River just north of Gansevoort Street. Currently, only one unmarked block remains, currently used as a garbage truck access behind the Bloomfield Street Sanitation Depot. The street was once longer, but much of the land it was built on was removed to provide longer piers for berthing larger ships, such as [RMS _Lusitania_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMS_Lusitania "RMS Lusitania") and [RMS _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic "Titanic"), without protruding further into the Hudson River. [Twelfth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Side_Highway "West Side Highway") is the highest numbered avenue that is signed by the city and accessible to the public. Higher-numbered avenues exist in other boroughs.

[Sixth and a Half Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_and_a_Half_Avenue "Sixth and a Half Avenue") is the only numbered avenue in Manhattan involving [fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraction "Fraction").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-11)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]

#### Philadelphia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Numbered_street&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Philadelphia")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Map_of_the_Original_City_of_Philadelphia_in_1682_by_Thomas_Holme.jpg/250px-Map_of_the_Original_City_of_Philadelphia_in_1682_by_Thomas_Holme.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_the_Original_City_of_Philadelphia_in_1682_by_Thomas_Holme.jpg)

Original street plan of [Center City Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_City,_Philadelphia "Center City, Philadelphia")

[Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_City,_Philadelphia "Center City, Philadelphia")[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") was laid out by [Thomas Holme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holme "Thomas Holme") in 1683[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-virginia-12) and was the first city to use numbered streets systematically. While the original plan had two sets of north–south numbered streets, one parallel to the [Delaware River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_River "Delaware River") and one to the [Schuylkill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schuylkill_River "Schuylkill River"); all are now numbered from the Delaware, with numbers increasing westward and continuing across the Schuylkill through [West Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Philadelphia "West Philadelphia") to the edge of the city. There are two main exceptions to this pattern: Holme's plan included [Front Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Street_(Philadelphia) "Front Street (Philadelphia)") in place of First and [Broad Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Street_(Philadelphia) "Broad Street (Philadelphia)") in place of Fourteenth; "Schuylkill Front Street" became 22nd when the streets west of Broad were renumbered. The highest numbered street is 90th Street.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-gm-13) In [Southwest Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Philadelphia "Southwest Philadelphia"), the grid is oblique, with numbered streets running from northwest to southeast and meeting their West Philadelphia equivalents at Baltimore Avenue. In general, numbered streets northwest of the Schuylkill are not aligned with their counterparts across the river in [South Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Philadelphia "South Philadelphia").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-google3-14)

The [Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington,_Philadelphia "Kensington, Philadelphia") area has streets lettered "A" through "O". The [East Oak Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Oak_Lane "East Oak Lane") and [West Oak Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Oak_Lane "West Oak Lane") sections of the city contains east–west streets numbered from 64th Avenue to 80th Avenue, with the numbers correspondent with the block numbers north from [Market Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_Street_(Philadelphia) "Market Street (Philadelphia)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-adcphiladelphia-15)

In the early 20th century, many of [Chestnut Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chestnut_Hill,_Philadelphia "Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia")'s previously numbered streets were renamed for [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") tribes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-google4-16)

#### Phoenix

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Numbered_street&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Phoenix")]

In [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), the north-south streets used a numbered system, with the center street being Central Avenue. Streets west of Central Avenue are named "avenue", thus, for example, 33rd Avenue is the thirty-third street west of Central Avenue. Streets east of Central Avenue are named "street", thus, for example, 27th Street is the twenty-seventh street east of Central Avenue. These streets and avenues are further divided into, for example, "North 9th Street" and "South 9th Street", with the dividing line being a line extending from Washington Street. East-west streets are not named using a numbered system.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-phoenixmap-17) Adjacent municipalities, such as [Glendale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale,_Arizona "Glendale, Arizona") and [Peoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peoria,_Arizona "Peoria, Arizona"), continue this grid system, although there are exceptional streets that do not follow the numbered street convention.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-phoenixmap-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-18)

In the city of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), the numbered streets were originally named streets that were perpendicular to the [Allegheny River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_River "Allegheny River"). [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") has two numbered series: streets, which run generally east–west, and avenues, which are north–south. The two series do not meet, nor are house numbers coordinated with cross streets' numbers.

The numbered streets begin with 1st Street in [SoMa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoMa "SoMa") and end with 30th Street in [Noe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noe_Valley "Noe Valley"). Some of these streets are only nominally east–west, which causes anomalies such as [3rd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Street_(San_Francisco) "Third Street (San Francisco)") meeting 26th Street in the [Dogpatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogpatch,_San_Francisco "Dogpatch, San Francisco").

The numbered avenues are in the [Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_District,_San_Francisco "Richmond District, San Francisco") and [Sunset Districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset_District,_San_Francisco "Sunset District, San Francisco") beginning with 2nd Avenue and continuing westward to 48th Avenue, which runs parallel to the Pacific Ocean shore.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Gallery_Place.jpg/250px-Gallery_Place.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gallery_Place.jpg)

[Pierre L'Enfant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_L'Enfant "Pierre L'Enfant")'s plan for [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") includes both radial avenues and grid system consisting of both numbered and lettered streets. North–south streets are named with numbers, such as "[7th Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Street_(Washington,_D.C.) "7th Street (Washington, D.C.)")," and west–east streets are named with letters, such as "[H Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H_Street_(Washington,_D.C.) "H Street (Washington, D.C.)")." The name is then followed with a directional suffix (NW, NE, SW, or SE), specifying a quadrant of the city (e.g. B Street Southwest). The quadrants meet at the [U.S. Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Capitol "U.S. Capitol") building.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numbered_street#cite_note-google5-21)

Within the city, the quadrants are divided by three streets known as _[North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North\_Capitol\_Street "North Capitol Street")_, _[East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East\_Capitol\_Street "East Capitol Street")_, and _[South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South\_Capitol\_Street "South Capitol Street")_**Capitol Streets**, and by the [National Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mall "National Mall"), which takes the place of the non-existent _West Capitol Street_. Numbers start counting upward on either side of North and South Capitol Streets, and letters start counting upward on either side of East Capitol Street and the National Mall.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
